{"pane_id":"w3W:pB","label":"research: new cloudflare cli","agent":"research-new-cloudflare-cli","status":"done","message":"## 1. `cf` (the new Cloudflare CLI)

URL: https://github.com/cloudflare/cf · announcement https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-cf-cli-launch/ (fetched through the mirror at noise.getoto.net)

- **Identity**
  - The npm package is `cf` (binaries `cf` and `cloudflare`). The latest is `1.0.0-beta.12`, published 2026-10-02 (registry.npmjs.org, verified). Licence is MIT OR Apache-2.0.
  - Open beta announced 2026-09-28 (announcement mirror; the blog itself did not load for me). The package README links a second post, `blog.cloudflare.com/cf-cli-local-explorer/`, which describes a "technical preview" via `npx cf`. The two posts disagree on the label.
  - It is actively maintained: 12 betas in about a week, and the repository was pushed to on 2026-10-04 (GitHub API).
- **C1 (status, relation to wrangler)**
  - Open beta. Cloudflare describes it as the successor and eventual replacement for wrangler (announcement; documentation-level).
  - When the beta ends, Cloudflare ships a final wrangler major that points users to `cf`, then gives 18 months of maintenance (announcement).
  - `cf migrate` converts a wrangler project (trial: `--dry-run`, `--bundler vite|wrangler`).
  - Its API surface is generated from the OpenAPI schema, about 3,000 operations against wrangler's roughly 280 (announcement).
- **C2 (D1 migrations)**
  - Trial: `cf d1 migrations` exists, described as "Create, list, and apply D1 database migrations".
  - The README says `--local` supports "D1 raw plus D1 migration list/apply". I could not read the flags of the subcommands, because `-h` on them printed the root help.
  - Not verified: file format, tracking table, rollback, and whether `create` works locally.
  - `cf d1 time-travel` exists (trial).
- **C3 (deploy, bindings)**
  - Trial: `cf deploy` has `--prebuilt`, `--tag`, `--message`, `--secrets-file`, `--dry-run`, `--dispatch-namespace` and `--containers-rollout immediate|gradual|none`. `cf containers` and `cf workers versions create` also exist.
  - Config moves to a typed `cloudflare.config.ts`, with a `bindings` helper that lists D1, R2, KV, Queues, Vectorize, AI and worker-to-worker bindings (announcement). Workflows bindings in the config are not confirmed.
  - The default build tool is Vite. The announcement says `cf` "will continue to delegate builds to Wrangler" for projects that need it, with Python Workers named as an example. It documents no Python Worker flow.
  - The `cf init` template is a TypeScript Worker (README).
- **C4 (local development)**
  - `cf dev` runs the framework's dev command or an installed Cloudflare dev server (trial).
  - `--local` runs a command against a Miniflare instance with persisted state. Cold-state support is stated for KV, D1 raw and migration list/apply, and R2 object get/upload/list/bulk delete (README). Some Durable Object and Workflow operations need a live peer.
  - A "Local Explorer" lets you inspect KV, R2, D1, Durable Objects and Workflows (the cf-cli-local-explorer post, as summarized by a fetch).
- **C5 (CI)**
  - The `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` environment variable is checked first, then OAuth profiles (README). `cf auth create|delete|activate|deactivate|list|login|logout` manage the profiles.
  - I found no official GitHub Action for `cf`. The docs I fetched mention only `wrangler-action`.
  - `cf init .` is the documented non-interactive form.

## 2. wrangler (baseline)

URL: https://github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk · npm `wrangler`

- **Version and maintenance**
  - Latest is 4.147.0, published 2026-10-02 (registry). The project pins 4.135.0.
  - It is maintained, and the planned 18-month maintenance window comes after the `cf` beta ends.
- **C1**
  - GA. It is the current Cloudflare Workers CLI.
  - `cf` is planned to replace it, and `cf` can delegate builds to it.
- **C2 (D1 migrations)** (docs: developers.cloudflare.com/d1/reference/migrations/ and /workers/wrangler/commands/d1/)
  - Migrations are hand-written `.sql` files in a `migrations/` folder. `wrangler d1 migrations create` makes an empty numbered file.
  - `list` and `apply` accept `--local` and `--remote`. The confirmation prompt is skipped in CI.
  - Applied names are tracked in the `d1_migrations` table. The table name and `migrations_dir` are configurable in the D1 binding, and `migrations_pattern` is a glob for nested layouts.
  - There is no down-migration or rollback command. A migration that errors is rolled back, and earlier ones stay applied. Backups are taken after a successful apply, and `d1 time-travel info|restore` gives point-in-time recovery.
- **C3**
  - `wrangler deploy` uses `wrangler.toml`/`.jsonc` and covers D1, R2, Queues, Workflows, service bindings and Containers. Your pipeline already deploys this way (trial on your repo's setup, not re-run here).
  - Python Workers use `pywrangler` (`uvx --from workers-py pywrangler init`, then `uv run pywrangler deploy`) and the `python_workers` compatibility flag (docs).
  - The Python docs list KV, D1, Durable Objects, R2, Workflows, Queues, Workers AI, Vectorize and service bindings as available. They never mention `cf`.
- **C4**
  - `wrangler dev` runs Workers locally and simulates D1 and R2 with Miniflare. This is documented, and I did not run it here.
  - `--local` is the default for the D1 migration commands.
- **C5**
  - Authenticate with `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`.
  - The official action is `cloudflare/wrangler-action@v4`; the latest release is v4.1.3, published 2026-09-24 (docs and GitHub API).

## Alembic driving D1

- **`sqlalchemy-cloudflare-d1`**
  - Version 0.4.1, published 2026-10-02 (PyPI); 0.4.0 was published 2026-09-19. Repository https://github.com/collierking/sqlalchemy-cloudflare-d1 has 24 stars and was pushed to on 2026-10-02. It requires `sqlalchemy>=2.0`.
  - It connects either over the D1 REST API (sync and async) or through a Python Worker binding (`create_engine_from_binding`) (README).
  - Trial: I inspected the 0.4.1 wheel. It contains no mention of "alembic" and no Alembic implementation class.
  - Its README states there are no transactions (every statement auto-commits), and `commit`/`rollback` are no-ops in `connection.py`. An Alembic run would have no rollback if a migration fails halfway.
- **Other routes**
  - Search found no package that connects Alembic to D1.
  - `sqlalchemy-d1` (a separate project, per search results) pins `sqlalchemy<2`. I did not open it.
  - D1's native migrations are SQL files applied by wrangler or `cf`, tracked in `d1_migrations`. Alembic can generate SQL with `alembic upgrade --sql` (offline mode), and the output could be placed in those files. I did not test that.

## Cross-cutting

- Both CLIs read `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` from the environment.
- Neither has a documented D1 rollback command beyond Time Travel.
- D1 migration files are plain SQL under both.

## Could not verify

- `cf d1 migrations` flags, file format, tracking table, and `--remote` behaviour (the help output printed the root help).
- Whether `cf` handles Python Workers, Containers config, Workflows bindings or service bindings in `cloudflare.config.ts` beyond the announcement's wording.
- Any official GitHub Action for `cf`.
- The `cf` docs site (developers.cloudflare.com/cf/); the announcement mirror is a secondary source.
- Alembic running against `sqlalchemy-cloudflare-d1`. I did not run it.

The research contradicts part of decision 10: staying in Python doesn't by itself keep Alembic working. The only SQLAlchemy driver for D1 has no Alembic support and no transactions. Alembic's offline mode (`alembic upgrade --sql`) could write migrations as SQL files for D1's own migration commands, but no one has tried that yet.

**Alembic against D1**
- `sqlalchemy-cloudflare-d1` 0.4.1 was published 2026-10-02; 0.4.0 came out on 2026-09-19. The project has 24 stars. The researcher inspected the 0.4.1 package and found no Alembic code in it.
- Its README says every statement commits on its own, and its `commit` and `rollback` do nothing. A migration that fails halfway would leave the schema half-applied.
- No other package connects Alembic to D1. A separate `sqlalchemy-d1` project pins SQLAlchemy below 2.0, and the API uses SQLAlchemy 2.

**The new CLI, `cf`**
- It's an open beta, announced 2026-09-28; the latest release is `1.0.0-beta.12` from 2026-10-02. A second Cloudflare post calls it a "technical preview".
- Cloudflare presents it as the eventual replacement for wrangler. When the beta ends, wrangler gets a final major release and 18 more months of maintenance.
- `cf migrate` converts a wrangler project. The configuration becomes a typed `cloudflare.config.ts`.
- It has a `cf d1 migrations` command, but the researcher couldn't read its flags or file format.
- For Python Workers, `cf` hands the build to wrangler. It documents no Python flow of its own, and its project template is a TypeScript Worker.
- It runs locally against Miniflare (D1, R2, KV). It has no official GitHub Action yet. It authenticates with `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, as wrangler does.

**wrangler**
- It's GA. The latest is 4.147.0; the pipeline pins 4.135.0.
- D1 migrations are hand-written `.sql` files tracked in a `d1_migrations` table, applied with `--local` or `--remote`. A failed migration is rolled back on its own, but there is no command to undo an applied migration; restoring with Time Travel is the only way back.
- Python Workers deploy through `pywrangler`. Its GitHub Action is `wrangler-action` v4.1.3.

The settled decisions are unchanged.

Questions this raises:
- For the Python options, should the spike try Alembic writing SQL files for D1's migration commands, or should migrations move to hand-written SQL?
- Should the spike deploy with `cf` (beta, hands Python builds to wrangler) or with wrangler?

The two questions about the spike from my last message, which parts and which deferred-work service, are still open.

- we should attempt both mechanism for migrations
- let's use wrangler for now
- let's test all the parts you mentioned above to understand if they work with workers, containers and eventually a typescript migrations
- I'm leaning towards workflows, and we can integrate a single pipeline that does the whole thing no?

can you do a quick pro/cons analysis of each approach (worker, container, typescript worker) and each of the backgorund tasks approaches

• D1, R2, Workflows, Queues and service bindings are native
• Scales to zero; no container to keep warm

• Work that dies still needs `queued_at` and the retry route to recover | | **Queues** | • Retried messages; each consumer run gets up to 15 min
• Fits "do this one step later" | • One message is one unit of work: a multi-step flow chains messages, or tracks its own state | | **Workflows** | • Durable steps with a retry per step; a crash resumes from the last finished step
• The pipeline already uses one, so the team knows it | • Python access to Workflows is reported but unverified
• Limits on step count, step output size and sleep aren't researched; audio comes back from Modal base64-encoded in one poll, so the output size limit matters | | **Durable Object alarms** | • One object per item could hold that item's state and wake itself to poll | • You write the retries and the scheduling yourself
• From a Container it goes through the Worker in front | ## One Workflow for the whole item It could be done: fetch, extract, describe, TTS, then store, as steps of one durable run instead of the API advancing the item on each `GET /items/{id}`. What that would change: - **Status updates:** the item's state would be written to D1 by the Workflow, and polling would become a read. - **Invariant 5:** "no worker, deferred work dies with the container" stops being true; Workflows' durable retries replace `queued_at` and the retry route. - **Where the Workflow lives:** the extraction Workflow is in `pipeline/`, so one Workflow spanning both `api/` and `pipeline/` sits across two deployables. Today's invariant 8 keeps those shipping independently. The other option is a Workflow in the API that calls the extraction Workflow as one step. - **Per-domain queue:** `DomainQueue` puts jobs for the same domain in a line ahead of extraction. A merged Workflow would have to wait on it, or the queue would move. - **Modal:** a Workflow step would sleep and poll Modal, so either the `modal` client or the HTTP endpoints would have to be reachable from where that step runs. Questions this raises: - Does the item Workflow live in `api/`, in `pipeline/`, or does the split between the two change? - Should I research Workflows' limits (step output size, step count, sleep, calling from Python) before the spike?

I applied three of your four notes on the canvas:
- **Spacing:** option C's full diagram now has room below its title.
- **External services:** Firecrawl, the image hosts, Gemini and Modal are clouds in every drawing, not only option C.
- **Client:** it's an ellipse everywhere, so squares are only our own modules.

**The note beside option C's full diagram is gone.** It was the one saying every step writes status to D1 and image processing runs in the Workflow. I didn't delete it on purpose, and I can't tell whether you removed it or my cleanup of the sticky notes did. I can put it back.

**Your other note asked whether the API could become TypeScript too, since it's thin. Yes: if the Workflow does all the item work, almost nothing is left that needs Python.** Under option C with the full Workflow, the API keeps five jobs:
- checking `X-API-Key`
- `POST /items`: insert a row in D1 and start the Workflow
- `GET /items/{id}`: read the row from D1
- the audio and image routes: redirect to a presigned R2 URL
- `POST /items/{id}/retry`

Everything that tied the API to Python moves into the Workflow under that option: the `modal` client, cairosvg and Pillow, `firecrawl-py` and `google-genai`. What a TypeScript API Worker would change:
- It reaches D1 and the Workflow directly through bindings, with no front Worker, Durable Object or container in between.
- It runs in the same language and tooling as `pipeline/`.
- Two things are unresearched: presigning R2 URLs from TypeScript, and whether an R2 binding can presign at all.

Two settled decisions conflict with this:
- **Decision 9 dropped the TypeScript Worker.** A TypeScript API would reopen it.
- **Decision 10 assumes the API stays in Python.** A TypeScript API ends Alembic, so migrations would be hand-written SQL for wrangler.

**"Thin" also depends on a question that's still open.** The API is only this thin if describing and the TTS call also run in the Workflow; if they call back into the Python API, that work stays in the API.

The settled set hasn't changed.

Questions this raises:
- Is the TypeScript API a fifth option to draw and spike next to A–D, or does it replace C?
- Do describing and the TTS call run in the Workflow, in TypeScript?

{"pane_id":"w3W:pD","label":"research: workflow languages","agent":"research-workflow-languages","status":"done","message":"# Languages for Cloudflare Workflows

Sources are tagged [docs] (Cloudflare documentation, fetched 2026-10-04) or [source] (GitHub API). No trials were run. Every claim below is documentation or repository metadata, not a verified fact.

## 1. TypeScript/JavaScript Workflows
https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/workers-api/

- **W1:**
  - The Workflow class is authored by extending `WorkflowEntrypoint` and implementing `run(event, step)`. [docs]
  - It is the reference implementation: `step.do` (retries and rollback config), `step.sleep`, `step.sleepUntil` and `step.waitForEvent` (default timeout 24h, resumed by `instance.sendEvent()`). [docs]
  - Status: public beta from 2024-10-23, GA from 2025-04-07. [docs, changelog]
  - A Workflow can also be declared in `exports` with `type: "workflow"` and called through `ctx.exports.<Name>`. [docs]
- **W2:**
  - A cross-script Workflow binding uses the `script_name` field, so a Worker in another script can bind to this Workflow. [docs]
  - Service bindings are asynchronous and must be awaited. [docs] The service bindings page does not say which Worker languages can sit on either side.
  - No page says whether a binding from a non-JS Worker to a JS Workflow is supported or unsupported.

## 2. Python Workflows (Python Workers)
https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/python/

- **W1:**
  - The Workflow class can be authored in Python by exporting a `WorkflowEntrypoint` (`from workers import WorkflowEntrypoint`) with `async def run(self, event, step)`. [docs, last updated 2026-09-17]
  - Steps are declared as `@step.do('name', config={...})`, with `concurrent` and `depends=[...]` options. Implicit dependency resolution by parameter name is preferred for new Workflows. `step.sleep`, `step.sleep_until` and `step.wait_for_event` (24h default timeout) exist. [docs, python-workers-api page]
  - Status: "Python Workflows is now in open beta" on 2025-08-22. [docs, changelog] No later GA entry appears in the changelog I fetched. The Python SDK pages state no status.
- **W2:**
  - A Python Worker creates instances with `await self.env.MY_WORKFLOW.create()`, "like you would on a JavaScript worker". `env` is a JsProxy of the JS object. [docs]
  - The docs state no restriction on Python/JS interop. They also state no explicit support for a Python Worker binding to a JS Workflow, or the reverse.

## 3. Other languages
- **Rust via workers-rs**
  - **W1:** No. `WorkflowEntrypoint` is not supported in workers-rs. The "Workflows support" issue #663 has been open since 2024-10-25. [source] PR #918 "feat: add Workflows support" (opened 2026-01-28) is open and unmerged, last updated 2026-09-18. [source] The latest workers-rs release is v0.8.7, published 2026-09-25. [source] The Rust docs page I grepped lists no Workflow binding type. [docs]
  - **W2:** A Rust Worker can be called by a Workflow step through a service binding (the generic mechanism). I did not find this documented for Rust specifically.
- **WASM-compiled code**
  - The Workflows docs list no WASM-authored Workflow. I found no page that says either way. A TypeScript Workflow could call a WASM module in-process from a step. I did not verify this.
- **Container called from a step**
  - **W1:** Not applicable. A container does not author the Workflow class.
  - **W2:**
    - Containers are reached through a Durable Object binding: `getContainer(env.X, id)`, or `ctx.container` inside a `DurableObject`. [docs]
    - The Workflows docs I fetched do not mention Containers or call one from a step. The Containers docs I fetched did not state GA or beta status, or which Worker languages can invoke them. A step can call the Durable Object binding like any other binding, but that is an inference, not a documented claim.

## W3: Limits (apply to all Workflows, language-independent) [docs, limits page, last updated 2026-09-21]

| Limit | Free | Paid |
|---|---|---|
| Non-stream step result | 1 MiB | 1 MiB |
| Steps per instance | 1,024 | 10,000 default, configurable up to 25,000 |
| Max sleep | 365 days | 365 days |
| CPU time per step | 10 ms | 30 s default, configurable up to 5 min |
| Wall time per step | unlimited | unlimited |
| Retention of completed instance state | 3 days | 30 days |
| State size per instance | 100 MB | 1 GB |
| Concurrent instances | 100 | 50,000 (waiting instances don't count) |
| Subrequests per request | 50 | 10,000 default, up to 10 million |

- Event payload is limited to 1 MiB.
- Paid plans can create 300 instances per second per account, and have a 2,000,000 queued-instance cap.
- `step.sleep` does not count toward the step limit. [docs]
- JS steps can return a `ReadableStream<Uint8Array>` for large binary output (changelog 2026-03-26). That output is excluded from the 1 MiB limit, which applies to "non-stream" results. [docs]
- The limits page does not distinguish JS from Python. Whether the Python SDK supports stream returns is unverified.

## Cross-cutting
- Every Workflow runs on Workers. The class is authored in JS/TS or Python only; Rust is not supported.
- A step is ordinary Worker code. Anything it can reach through bindings (service bindings, Durable Object bindings, R2, D1, `fetch` to Modal) is available regardless of the language on the other side.

## Not verified
- Whether Python Workflows is still beta as of 2026-10-04. No GA entry was found, and the SDK pages state no status.

Workflows can be written in TypeScript/JavaScript or Python. Rust, WebAssembly and containers can't define a Workflow, but a step can call out to code in any language. None of this was tried; it comes from Cloudflare's docs and GitHub.

**By language**
- **TypeScript/JavaScript:** GA since 2025-04-07, with the full step API (`step.do`, `step.sleep`, `step.waitForEvent`). The pipeline already uses it.
- **Python:** open beta since 2025-08-22, and the researcher found no later GA entry.
  - It has the same step API, written with Python decorators (`@step.do`, `step.sleep`, `step.wait_for_event`).
  - It runs on Python Workers (Pyodide), with that package list: Pillow is there, while cairosvg and the `modal` client aren't.
- **Rust:** not supported. The workers-rs issue asking for Workflows has been open since 2024-10-25, and the pull request adding it hasn't been merged.
- **WebAssembly:** the docs don't mention it either way.

**Mixing languages**
- A step is ordinary Worker code. It can call anything it has a binding for: another Worker in another language, a Container through its Durable Object, R2, D1, or a plain HTTP request to Modal.
- A Workflow can be started from a Worker in a different script.
- Whether that works across languages (a Python Worker starting a TypeScript Workflow, or the reverse) isn't documented either way.
- A step calling a Container isn't described in the docs either. It should work through the Durable Object binding, but that's my inference.

**Limits that apply to option C**

| | Paid plan |
|---|---|
| Value a step returns | 1 MiB, but a JS step can return a stream instead, which doesn't count toward that limit |
| Steps per instance | 10,000 by default, up to 25,000 |
| CPU time per step | 30 s by default, up to 5 min |
| Wall time per step | Unlimited |
| Longest sleep | 365 days; sleeps don't count as steps |
| How long finished instances are kept | 30 days |

**Two of these limits matter for option C's steps:**
- **Audio:** Modal returns the audio base64-encoded in the poll result, and a few MB of audio is over 1 MiB. The poll step would have to write it to R2 itself, or return it as a stream.
- **Image processing:** the 30 s CPU default limits how long one step can spend converting and re-encoding images.

17. The API stays a separate deployable in `api/`, outside `pipeline/`.
18. The modules inside `pipeline/` may be reorganized to keep each part separate.

## Unknowns in the chosen design
1. **Image processing in a TypeScript Worker.** Can WebAssembly libraries turn SVG into PNG and re-encode to WebP inside a Worker? The limits that apply are 128 MB of memory per isolate, 30 s of CPU per step by default (5 min at most), and the bundle size cap. If not, the fallback container from decision 12 is used.
2. **Modal over HTTP.** This needs two web endpoints in `tts/` and a way to protect them. Audio comes back base64-encoded and is larger than the 1 MiB a step can return. So either the polling step writes it to R2 itself, or it returns it as a stream.
3. **Shape of the item Workflow.** This covers how the sleep-and-poll loop counts against the step limit, and the retry settings for each step. It also covers how step 2 waits for the domain's lease: DomainQueue was built to start one extraction Workflow per job, not to hold the lease for a step inside another Workflow.
4. **Starting a Workflow from another deployable.** The API Worker starts the item Workflow in `pipeline/` through a Workflow binding that names the other script. This has to work in production, in local development, and whichever of the two deploys first.
5. **One D1 database written by two Workers.** It's bound in both `api/` and `pipeline/`. Open points are the conditional updates (`meta.changes`), which deployable owns the hand-written migrations, and how they're applied in CI.
6. **Presigned R2 URLs from TypeScript.** It's unknown which library signs them, and whether an `<audio>` element plays the URL after the API's 307 redirect.
7. **Gemini and Firecrawl from a Worker.** Their JavaScript SDKs, or plain requests, have to run inside Workers.
8. **Local development and tests.** Both Workers would run locally with D1 and R2 simulated, with the binding between them working. The current test suite replays HTTP calls through vcrpy; a TypeScript suite would need a replacement.

Rewriting the spoken-form logic and the item contract in TypeScript isn't on this list. That's porting work, not an unknown. The invariants it has to keep (1–3, on how units and timing line up) carry over unchanged.

## How the spike would run
- **Coordinator:** one Opus subagent in its own herdr tab. It hands each unknown to a child subagent, runs the independent ones in parallel, collects the results, and writes one report into the change's scratch folder.
- **Children:** one per unknown, each with its own throwaway worktree and branch, deploying to Cloudflare under spike-only names. Each reports whether its unknown works, what it measured, and what failed.
- **Order:** unknowns 1, 2, 6 and 7 don't depend on anything and can run in parallel. 3, 4 and 5 build on each other. 8 comes last, once the pieces exist.
- **Throwaway:** spike code never merges. What it settles goes back to you as findings.

Running this is `mahou:spike`'s job, not this exploration's. I can open it once the plan is settled.

Questions for the plan:

# Cloudflare Workflows: spawn-and-resolve and its limits

verified: 2026-09-13

Answers how to run a long job on Cloudflare Workflows from another service in a spawn-and-resolve shape, what the hard limits are, and which creation semantics are safe to retry. Distilled from a survey run while designing an extraction service against Cloudflare Workflows.

## Knowledge

- Instances get caller-chosen ids: `env.WORKFLOW.create({ id, params })`, ids up to 100 chars matching `^[a-zA-Z0-9_][a-zA-Z0-9-_]*$` (REST also reserves `cf_` + 64 hex). Mapping instances to your own identifiers is a documented use, and `params` is any JSON value.
- `create()` is not idempotent: it throws when the id exists within the retention window (3 days free, 30 paid, configurable per instance). `createBatch()` is idempotent and skips existing ids. Create-or-resume is two operations: create, catch the exists error, then `get(id)`; `get()` throws for an unknown id, so an id that does not resolve yet can mean queued-behind-something rather than absent.
- The finished `run()` return value is fetchable as the instance's `output` through `instance.status()` from a Worker route, or through the REST GET-instance endpoint, which also returns a per-step array with attempts and timings. The status set is queued, running, paused, errored, terminated, complete, waiting, waitingForPause, unknown.
- Wall clock per instance is unlimited. The binding constraint is CPU per step invocation: 10 ms on the free plan, 30 s default and configurable to 5 minutes via `limits.cpu_ms`. Waiting on network I/O does not burn CPU, so a job of many slow model calls fits; a single heavy parse must fit the CPU budget.
- Payloads: params, events and non-stream step results are each capped at 1 MiB. Larger artifacts go to external storage (R2) with a reference passed instead. Whether `run()`'s final output shares the 1 MiB cap is undocumented.
- Steps run once durably via `step.do`; the return value is persisted and replayed on resume instead of re-executing. Branching is plain JS control flow inside `run()`. Steps support per-step retries (limit up to 10,000, fixed or backoff delay) and a per-attempt timeout; `NonRetryableError` stops retrying; `step.sleep` waits up to 365 days; `step.waitForEvent` waits from 1 second to 365 days.
- Concurrency: instances with different ids run concurrently; sleeping or event-waiting instances do not count toward the running cap (50,000 paid, 100 free), so millions can wait at once. Creates are rate-limited per account (300/s paid).
- Conflicting limits exist across Cloudflare's own docs: the Agents SDK page says 10 MB state per workflow and 30 minutes per step; the Workflows reference says 100 MB to 1 GB per instance and unlimited step wall clock. The Workflows reference matches observed behavior reports; treat the Agents SDK table as stale.

## Sources

- Workers API (updated 2026-08-12): https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/workers-api/
- Limits (updated 2026-06-15): https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/reference/limits/
- Trigger Workflows (updated 2026-07-13): https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/trigger-workflows/
- Sleeping and retrying (updated 2026-07-09): https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/sleeping-and-retrying/
- REST instances create/get: https://developers.cloudflare.com/api/resources/workflows/subresources/instances/

# Cassettes over mocks

The api suite replays a service behind an HTTP boundary, the extraction pipeline, from cassettes exactly as it replays firecrawl and gemini, so the client's real serialization and parsing run against the recorded shapes. Mocks are for calls that are not plain HTTP.

- Record against the real service when it can run: `wrangler dev` needs no account and serves on localhost. The conftest's matching rules carry the hard parts: body matching disambiguates POSTs to one URL, and repeated identical GETs replay in recorded order, which is a poll sequence.
- Fabricate when the service does not exist yet: a cassette is YAML of request and response pairs, hand-built from the boundary contract. The trade is that a recorded cassette is evidence the service answered, and a fabricated one is the contract restated as a fixture, so drift passes unnoticed. Both sides are ours, so the risk is small.
- The unreachable case cannot be a cassette: a refused connection produces no interaction. Point the client at 127.0.0.1, a closed port that refuses instantly, with recording disabled for that one test. The failure is a genuine network one.
- Mocks stay for what is not HTTP: modal's spawn-and-resolve, the gemini describer SDK.
- Volatile ids break replay: minted `itm_` handles differ per run. A registered matcher normalizes them on both sides, cassette and request, so one cassette replays across any mint.

# Spike

A spike is code written to answer a question. The answer is the product; the code is not. You build it small, run it against reality, and throw it away. It never merges, never the starting point of the real implementation, which gets built clean once the question is settled.

## The process

1. **Name the question.** One design question that reading and asking cannot settle: whether an approach holds, what shape something should take, what actually happens when the real thing runs. A question a document or a scout can answer does not need a spike.

2. **Build the smallest working version of the real thing.** It works, against real inputs, under real conditions. A mock answers nothing. Build only what the question asks about. Build it in the change's scratch folder, at `spikes/<question-slug>/`, so nothing of it touches a repository.

3. **Run it against reality and observe.** Whatever can tell you the answer is the reactor: real data, a real run, a person reacting, another agent attempting the task. You choose the reactor for the spike; it is not prescribed. What happens is the result, and the gap between that and what was expected is usually the finding.

4. **Iterate in rounds under a strategy.** A round changes something and produces an outcome; the outcome settles a decision or sharpens the question, and the next round builds on what settled. Load the strategy for changing things from `references/strategies/` and pick it per spike:

   | Strategy | When |
   |---|---|
   | [One variable per round](references/strategies/one-variable.md) | The question has a working baseline and the rounds narrow in on failures |
   | [Variants in parallel](references/strategies/variants-in-parallel.md) | Several answers could work and only evidence picks between them |

   A spike may invent its own strategy; when one works, it is a candidate for mahou:learn to add here.

5. **Stop when the question is answered.** Record the answer and the findings in the spike's folder. Every surprise is input to the design that follows. The artifacts stay as reference material for whoever builds the real thing.

## What a spike never does

It never decides for the user. The spike brings the outcome; the design decisions it raises go back as questions. It never grows a second question. A new question is a new spike. Extracting the real thing from spike code keeps every shortcut the throwaway allowed.

# One variable per round

The strategy for narrowing in on failures when a working baseline exists.

Each round changes one thing and re-runs. When the spike's output fails somewhere, fix that failing case alone. The fix must generalize, not special-case the case that happened to fail. After every fix, re-run everything that already passed. A fix that breaks a passing case has to be redone, and only the re-run can see it, because the failing case itself will look solved.

One variable per round keeps cause and effect readable. A round that changes three things produces an outcome nobody can attribute, and the next round builds on a guess.

The loop ends when the whole corpus passes, not when the last failing case does.

# Variants in parallel

The strategy for questions several answers could settle, where only evidence picks between them.

Build two or three variants, each one an answer to the question, and race them: the same inputs, the same measure of outcome, the same rounds. The variants differ in the one dimension the question is about, nothing else. A variant that differs in polish or effort measures nothing.

Pick the winner on the evidence the race produced, and the evidence is the finding: what the winner did that the losers did not, and what each loser got wrong. A losing variant that revealed a constraint no winner could see is worth as much as the winner.

The winner's artifact becomes the reference for the real implementation. Build that implementation clean rather than extracting it from the artifact.
